author: Great Lakes Wire
title: Attorney General Nessel warns of bank and credit union imposter scams
text:
Attorney General Nessel warns of bank and credit union imposter scams
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel reissued a consumer alert on Aug. 12, warning residents about imposter scams involving fraudsters posing as banks or credit unions to steal financial and personal information.
According to the Attorney General's office, scammers have used spoofing technology to make caller ID appear as if calls are coming from legitimate financial institutions. The callers may claim there is an issue with a consumer’s account, such as unauthorized transactions or overdrafts, and offer to resolve it. During these interactions, the scammer asks for account credentials or personal information that can be used to access and drain accounts.
“Bad actors rely on urgency and spoofing technology to trick Michigan consumers into giving up access to their hard-earned money,” said Attorney General Nessel. “If you receive an unexpected call claiming there is a problem with your account, hang up immediately and contact your bank or credit union directly. If you believe you’ve been a victim of one of these scams, my office is here to help.”
Patty Corkery, President/CEO of the Michigan Credit Union League, said, “Credit unions work diligently to provide alerts and educational resources to help members recognize and avoid fraud. One of the most important reminders is to never share passwords or PINs with anyone, even if the request appears to come from the credit union. Bank and credit union imposter scams are becoming increasingly common and sophisticated, and unfortunately, older Michiganders are often the primary targets. We encourage everyone to take advantage of the educational resources available through the state, local credit unions and TryACreditUnion.com to stay informed and protect against fraud.”
DIFS Director Anita Fox also commented, “Imposter scams continue to pose a serious threat to Michiganders, especially when fraudsters pretend to be trusted banks or credit unions in an attempt to steal personal and financial information. Legitimate financial institutions will never pressure you to share information by phone, text, or email. Your best defense is simple: never share any information with anyone who contacts you. If something feels off, stop and verify it directly with your financial institution.”
The Department of Insurance and Financial Services Fraud Investigation Unit investigates criminal activity related to insurance and financial markets in coordination with law enforcement agencies across Michigan. Residents can report suspicious activity online or by calling DIFS at 877-999-6442 during business hours.
